claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by short-range chemical ordering and nanoscale clustering.
Energetically favorable ordering occurs between specific pairs such as Al–Cr or Al–Fe.
Slow cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for more SRO and nanoscale clustering to form than rapid quenching.
The SRO and nanoscale clusters produced during cooling stabilize the phase and microstructure.
Greater SRO and clustering improve high-temperature strength.
Greater SRO and clustering improve oxidation or environmental resistance.
Greater SRO and clustering improve radiation tolerance.
Greater SRO and clustering improve cryogenic toughness.
Water quenching freezes in a more chemically disordered configuration than furnace cooling.
The more disordered quenched configuration has lower phase stability than the furnace-cooled configuration.
The controlled comparison uses the same 1100°C, 2-hour inert-atmosphere anneal followed by either furnace cooling or water quenching.
The furnace-cooled baseline will have enhanced SRO and clustering relative to the quenched material.
Diffuse-scattering XRD, TEM contrast, and APT can characterize the proposed differences in SRO and nanoscale clustering.
The quenched specimens will show significantly reduced SRO and clustering signatures relative to the furnace-cooled baseline.
The quenched specimens will show lower high-temperature strength, oxidation resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness than the furnace-cooled specimens.
Cooling rate is assumed to dominate the relevant microstructural evolution under the stated annealing conditions.
Cooling-induced differences in grain size or residual stress could confound attribution of property changes to SRO.
The hypothesis is falsified if quenching causes no statistically significant reduction in SRO or clustering, or if the predicted property degradation is absent.
